Connectome-constrained atrophy in AD and FTD syndromes

Schaefer 100/200/400; HCP SC and FC; communication models vs distance; five null models

2026-11-21

1 Summary

Question. Does cortical atrophy in AD and the FTD syndromes follow the connectome, or is it explained by spatial proximity? Which communication model on the structural connectome (SC) predicts it best, and does any beat a distance-only baseline?

Data. Seven group-level DBM atrophy maps (AD, MCI from ADNI; PD from PPMI; pooled FTD, bvFTD, svPPA, nfvPPA from NIFD); HCP SC and FC; Schaefer 100/200/400 (400 primary). No DLB map exists in the two Zenodo records; none was substituted.

Main findings (Schaefer-400; all hold at 100 and 200 unless stated).

  1. No communication model beats distance. A distance-only kernel exp(−d/λ) predicts each region’s atrophy from other regions’ atrophy best in every syndrome (r = 0.57–0.83). The best SC models (one-step SC, search information, heat kernel) reach r = 0.44–0.72. Zero of 49 model-vs-distance comparisons favour a model at FDR < 0.05 at any resolution; giving each model one fitted exponent only produces ties (Δr ≤ 0.04, n.s.).
  2. The best “diffusion” is one step. The network diffusion kernel’s fitted β sits at the low end of its grid, i.e. it collapses to direct neighbours. Diffusion efficiency (1/MFPT) is dominated by node strength and gives negative or near-zero r; it should not be read as a spreading model.
  3. SC effects are mostly geometry. Degree-preserving rewiring makes every SC model look significant (35/35 tests); geometry-preserving rewiring makes almost none significant (2/35). The exception is bvFTD, where path-based SC models (shortest-path efficiency, navigation) and long-range heat/communicability beat the geometry-preserving null. Atrophy in bvFTD and AD is also smoother on the real SC than on geometry-matched rewired SCs (graph Dirichlet energy, p = 0.001).
  4. FC carries signal beyond distance, mainly in FTD. FC’s partial correlation with atrophy beyond the distance kernel: bvFTD 0.23, pooled FTD 0.18, svPPA 0.13, AD 0.11 (spin p ≤ 0.017). Using only connections longer than 30 mm, FC predicts bvFTD (r = 0.51), FTD (0.44) and svPPA (0.29) atrophy, significant under all three spatial nulls at 400 parcels and under the variogram null at 100, 200 and 400; in AD the long-range FC signal is weak (r ≈ 0.09).
  5. Epicentres. AD: left and right medial/anterior temporal parcels. bvFTD: orbitofrontal cortex and anterior insula (bilateral Cont_PFCv_1 and LH FrOperIns_3 in the top 5; the expected check passes). svPPA: left temporal pole. nfvPPA: left frontal operculum, FEF/premotor and SMA. When the voxel map is mirrored left–right, nfvPPA’s epicentres and most of svPPA’s lose rank (left-specific), whereas bvFTD’s and AD’s keep it (not hemisphere-specific).
  6. Null models decide significance. Parcel-level spins make maps rougher at short range than the real map (short-range variogram ≈ 1.9× empirical), so they flag 27/42 model fits as significant; variogram-matched surrogates flag 3/42 and Moran spectral randomisation 11/42. Conclusions above rest on effects that survive the stricter nulls.
  7. Eigenmodes. Geometric (cortical-surface) eigenmodes reconstruct AD and MCI atrophy better than spatially matched surrogates; FC harmonics do so for bvFTD and pooled FTD. SC harmonics beat degree-rewired SCs but not geometry-rewired ones (except in nfvPPA).
  8. Laterality. The apparent left peak in bvFTD is an atlas artefact: at voxel level bvFTD is near-symmetric (laterality index −0.06), while svPPA and nfvPPA are left-lateralised (+0.11).
  9. Similarity. AD resembles MCI (r = 0.80) and, less, svPPA (0.48) and bvFTD (0.31); all FTD maps are mutually similar (spin FDR < 0.05; inflated by a shared NIFD control group); PD is unrelated to the others. Highly FC-connected hubs are less atrophic in bvFTD and pooled FTD (ρ ≈ −0.62, FDR q = 0.007); SC strength shows no association that survives FDR.

Interpretation. At group level, AD atrophy is explained by spatial proximity: no structural route or functional network adds much. bvFTD (and pooled FTD, svPPA) additionally follow long-range functional networks, with a smaller structural-topology effect in bvFTD. Because degree-only rewiring and spin nulls overstate network effects, claims of “connectome-shaped atrophy” need geometry-aware nulls and a distance baseline.

Novelty. A systematic search found no prior head-to-head comparison of SC communication models against a distance baseline across AD and the FTD variants with spatial and rewiring nulls (see “Novelty check”). The bvFTD neighbour-atrophy result replicates Shafiei et al. 2023 with an independent connectome and atlas.

connectomeR. The 0.2.0 tarball was never supplied. All needed functions were written and validated against bctpy, netneurotools and neuromaps; the network functions form the package pkg/netcomm, which passes R CMD check (0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 notes) and is ready to merge into connectomeR 0.3.0. connectomeR itself could not be updated or checked.

Two data caveats. The three FTD-variant maps are on an unusual scale (about ±1.5, vs ±16 for pooled FTD; the MINC copies agree); all analyses are scale-invariant, but the values should not be read as t until the authors confirm what was deposited. The template and atlas differ (ICBM 2009c symmetric vs FSL MNI152), see Limitations.

Atrophy maps. Voxel-wise deformation-based morphometry (DBM) t-maps, patients vs matched controls, on the ICBM152 2009c nonlinear symmetric template.

  • Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.7392621 (Dadar, 2022; CC-BY-4.0): AD and MCI (ADNI), PD (PPMI), pooled FTD (NIFD). The record cites: Dadar M, et al. White matter hyperintensities are associated with grey matter atrophy and cognitive decline in Alzheimer’s disease and frontotemporal dementia. Neurobiol Aging 2022;111:54–63.
  • Zenodo 10.5281/zenodo.10383493 (Dadar & Metz, 2023; CC-BY-4.0): bvFTD, svPPA, nfvPPA (filed as pnfaPPA), all NIFD. The record cites Dadar et al. 2022 (above) and Metz A, et al. Brain atrophy and white matter hyperintensities in frontotemporal dementia variants and their impact on cognition. CCNA Partners Forum and Science Days, March 2024 (conference presentation).
  • Neither record has a DLB map or a link to one (dlb_mentioned above is FALSE for both).

Connectomes. HCP group-level structural (SC) and functional (FC) matrices for Schaefer-100/200/400 from the ENIGMA toolbox (Larivière et al., Nat Methods 2021), commit b08974b. Only the data files were read.

Atlas. Schaefer et al. 2018 (Cereb Cortex), 7-network order, FSL MNI152 1 mm volumes and label tables from CBIG, commit 634f676.

scripts/00_get_data.sh reproduces every download and checks the md5 sums.

All seven t-maps share one 1 mm grid (all(attr(s1, "same_grid")) = TRUE). The atlas is on a different grid and orientation (LAS vs RAS). It was resampled to the t-map grid by nearest neighbour through world coordinates; the t-maps were not resampled. The resampling code (R/parcellate.R) returns the atlas unchanged when resampled to its own grid, and gives a result identical voxel for voxel to an independent nibabel implementation on the t-map grid (checked during development for Schaefer-400; all 400 labels survive).

The two templates are both “MNI” but not identical (2009c symmetric vs FSL 6th generation). No transform between them was applied; the residual misregistration is a few millimetres, which matters little at parcel level but adds to boundary blurring.

2.3 Connectome matrices

read_mat <- function(type, k) {
  X <- as.matrix(read.csv(file.path(paths$enigma_mat, sprintf("%sMatrix_ctx_schaefer_%d.csv", type, k)), header = FALSE))
  dimnames(X) <- NULL; X
}
mat_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(resolutions, function(k) do.call(rbind, lapply(c("struc", "func"), function(ty) {
  X <- read_mat(ty, k); u <- X[upper.tri(X)]
  data.frame(matrix = ifelse(ty == "struc", "SC", "FC"), parcels = k, symmetric = isSymmetric(X),
             diag_zero = all(diag(X) == 0), negative_edges = sum(u < 0), zero_edges = sum(u == 0),
             positive_edges = sum(u > 0), density = round(mean(u != 0), 3),
             min = signif(min(u), 3), max = signif(max(u), 3))
}))))

The SC matrices contain 1, 8, 14 negative edges (unique, upper triangle; twice as many entries in the full matrix) at 100, 200 and 400 parcels. In Step 2 they are set to 0 (zero_negative() in R/setup.R, a stand-in for connectomeR::handle_negative()). The FC matrices have no negative values; their minimum is 0, so they appear to have been thresholded upstream.

2.4 Sphere centroids for the spin test

Parcel centroids on the fsaverage5 sphere were computed from the ENIGMA files (surfaces/fsa5_sphere_{lh,rh}.gii, permutation_testing/annot/fsa5_{lh,rh}_schaefer_*.annot; note the annot files are under enigmatoolbox/permutation_testing/, not datasets/permutation_testing/). Because connectomeR/inst/validation/annot_centroids.py was not available, scripts/annot_centroids.py reimplements the usual method (Vasa et al. 2018): the mean of each parcel’s sphere vertices, snapped to the nearest vertex. The snapped vertex was the nearest vertex overall for 400/400 parcels. The spins built on these centroids were validated against neuromaps (see “Validation of the new functions”); the file should still be compared with the package script.

3 Parcellation and coverage

Parcel value = mean t over the parcel’s voxels on the t-map grid that have a finite, non-zero t (the maps are 0 outside their brain mask). Coverage = that voxel count divided by the parcel’s voxel count on the t-map grid. Atrophy is defined as −t.

cov400 <- s1[["400"]]$coverage
cov_summary <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(s1), function(k) {
  cv <- s1[[k]]$coverage
  data.frame(parcels = as.integer(k), min_coverage = round(min(cv$coverage_min), 3),
             median_coverage = round(median(cv$coverage_min), 3),
             parcels_below_50pct = sum(!cv$included),
             coverage_identical_across_maps = all(apply(cv[, grep("^coverage_[A-Za-z]", names(cv))], 1, function(r) diff(range(r)) == 0)))
}))

The AD map peaks in medial temporal cortex (Limbic_TempPole parcels at y ≈ −20, z ≈ −27, parahippocampal), lateral and anterior temporal cortex, and the precuneus/posterior cingulate (Default_pCunPCC). The bvFTD map peaks in the left anterior insula/frontal operculum (Cont_PFCv_1 at −34, 16, −8; SalVentAttn_FrOperIns), dorsomedial prefrontal/anterior cingulate (Default_PFCdPFCm) and orbitofrontal cortex (Limbic_OFC). Both match the expected patterns. Neither map is sign-flipped or empty.

net_order <- c("Vis", "SomMot", "DorsAttn", "SalVentAttn", "Limbic", "Cont", "Default")
prof <- a400 %>% select(hemi, network, all_of(syn)) %>%
  pivot_longer(all_of(syn), names_to = "syndrome", values_to = "atrophy") %>%
  group_by(syndrome, hemi, network) %>% summarise(atrophy = mean(atrophy, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>%
  mutate(network = factor(network, rev(net_order)), syndrome = factor(syndrome, syn))
ggplot(prof, aes(atrophy, network, shape = hemi)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "#a8a79f", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_point(size = 2.4, colour = col_main, fill = "#fcfcfb", stroke = 0.9) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c(LH = 16, RH = 21), name = "Hemisphere") +
  facet_wrap(~syndrome, scales = "free_x", ncol = 4) +
  labs(x = "Mean atrophy (-t)", y = NULL) + theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Mean atrophy (−t) by Schaefer network and hemisphere, Schaefer-400. Each panel has its own x-scale because the FTD-variant maps are on a much smaller scale (see Status).

The svPPA map is most atrophic in the left, then right, limbic network (temporal pole). The nfvPPA map is left-lateralized; at network level it is flat across left limbic, default, salience and dorsal-attention parcels, and its peak parcels are left FEF/premotor, SMA and anterior insula/IFG (table above). The PD map is weak and diffuse. All three fit the clinical syndromes.

The bvFTD map has the same spatial pattern as the pooled FTD map (r = 0.90), but values about 8 times smaller in parcel-level SD (about 10 times in voxel range). One possible reading is that the variant maps are standardized effect sizes or t-values divided by a constant, rather than t-statistics; that is a guess and should be checked with the authors. It does not affect any planned analysis, because all of them use correlations, ranks or weighted averages.

5 Step 2: methods

source("R/setup.R"); source("R/analysis.R"); source("R/results.R")
source("R/extensions.R")
res_k <- setNames(resolutions, resolutions)
D <- lapply(res_k, prep_resolution)
CC <- lapply(res_k, load_caches)
d4 <- D[["400"]]; c4 <- CC[["400"]]
syn <- colnames(d4$A)
primary <- c("AD", "bvFTD", "svPPA", "nfvPPA")
syn_lab <- function(x) factor(x, levels = syn)
fmt_p <- function(p) ifelse(is.na(p), "", ifelse(p < 0.001, "<0.001", sprintf("%.3f", p)))

Inputs. Atrophy a_i = −mean t per parcel (see “Parcellation and coverage”), seven maps. HCP SC with its 1/8/14 negative edges (100/200/400 parcels) set to 0; FC used as given (all entries ≥ 0). Euclidean distances between CBIG parcel centroids (MNI mm). Schaefer-400 is primary; 100 and 200 repeat everything.

connectomeR. The package tarball was not available. Following your instruction to go on, every function the analysis needs was written and validated before use (see “Validation of the new functions”). The network functions form a small R package, pkg/netcomm (communication models with C++ kernels, spin permutations, rewiring, variogram and Moran surrogates; roxygen documentation; 42 testthat expectations). R CMD check --no-manual on it returns Status: OK (0 errors, 0 warnings, 0 notes); the PDF manual was skipped because the container has no LaTeX. The files are written to be merged into connectomeR as R/communication.R for version 0.3.0. That merge, the version bump and the check of connectomeR itself need the 0.2.0 source.

Prediction rule. For a model matrix M, P_i = Σ_{j≠i} M_ij a_j / Σ_{j≠i} M_ij and the statistic is r(a, P). With M = SC (or FC) this is the neighbour atrophy N_i of Zeighami et al. (2015) and Shafiei et al. (2023).

Models on the SC. Shortest-path efficiency (1/weighted path length, lengths 1/w); weighted communicability expm(S^-1/2 W S^-1/2) (Crofts & Higham 2009); search information (Goñi et al. 2014), used as the shortest-path probability 2^−SI; navigation efficiency with Euclidean greedy routing (Seguin et al. 2018); diffusion efficiency 1/MFPT (Goñi et al. 2013). Asymmetric measures were symmetrised as (M + Mᵀ)/2. Two models with one fitted parameter: the distance-only kernel exp(−d/λ) (λ over 40 values, 2–200 mm), and, added here, the network diffusion (heat) kernel expm(−βL) of Raj et al. (2012), with L the normalised Laplacian of the SC (β over 25 values). Fitted parameters were chosen to maximise r and refitted inside every null surrogate and every rewired network, so the nulls account for the fitting.

Nulls (1,000 each). (1) Spin: Hungarian-reassigned rotations of fsaverage5 parcel centroids (Vasa/Markello method), atrophy permuted, all predictions recomputed. (2) Degree-preserving rewiring of the SC (Maslov–Sneppen, 10 swaps per edge, weights travel with edges), all models recomputed on each rewired network, atrophy unchanged. Extensions add (3) geometry-preserving rewiring, (4) variogram-matched surrogates and (5) Moran spectral randomisation. p-values are one-sided (null r ≥ observed r) for model fits and two-sided for paired differences. FDR (Benjamini–Hochberg) is applied across syndromes × models within each null.

Every communication model matches bctpy 0.6.1 or netneurotools 0.3.0 on the Schaefer-400 SC to floating-point precision. Two notes: bctpy’s search_information fails under NumPy 2, so the reference keeps bctpy’s own Floyd–Warshall and path retrieval and only flattens the returned path; navigation agrees exactly, including which pairs fail (94.0% of pairs succeed at 400 parcels). Spins match neuromaps’ Hungarian implementation in distribution. Degree-preserving rewiring moves 92% of edges and doubles the mean edge length; geometry-preserving rewiring keeps edge lengths and the weight–length relation but saturates at about 50% turnover.

9 D. Epicentres

ep <- epicentre_table(d4, c4)
flipN <- c4$flipped
ep_flip <- do.call(rbind, lapply(syn, function(s) { a <- flipN[, s]; sc <- epicentre_score(a, predict_from_model(d4$SC, a)); data.frame(syndrome = s, parcel = seq_along(a), rank_mirrored = rank(-sc, ties.method = "min")) }))

Reading the p-values: they are one-sided (is the observed r larger than the null r?). Diffusion efficiency gives negative r, yet small rewiring p-values, because rewired networks give even more negative r. That is not evidence of a network constraint. On large graphs, 1/MFPT is dominated by the target node’s stationary probability, i.e. its strength (von Luxburg et al. 2014, JMLR 15:1751), so the “prediction” collapses to a function of node strength:

P_diff <- predict_from_model(communication_models(d4$SC, d4$Dist)$diffusion, d4$A)
round(sapply(syn, function(s) cor(P_diff[, s], rowSums(d4$SC))), 2)
##     AD    MCI     PD    FTD  bvFTD  svPPA nfvPPA 
##  -0.10  -0.56  -0.22  -0.70  -0.67  -0.27  -0.64

The heat kernel’s fitted β is at or near the lowest grid value for most syndromes; as β → 0 the kernel converges to one-step, degree-normalised SC, so the best-fitting “diffusion” is no diffusion beyond direct neighbours.

spin_band <- c4$spin %>% filter(R == 0, model %in% E_models) %>% group_by(model, syndrome) %>%
  summarise(lo = quantile(r, 0.025, na.rm = TRUE), hi = quantile(r, 0.975, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop")
pe <- E_tab %>% mutate(model = as.character(model), syndrome = as.character(syndrome)) %>% left_join(spin_band, by = c("model", "syndrome")) %>%
  mutate(model = factor(model_labels[model], rev(model_labels[E_models])), syndrome = syn_lab(syndrome),
         sig = ifelse(q_spin < 0.05, "spin q < 0.05", "n.s."))
ggplot(pe, aes(r, model)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "#a8a79f", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = lo, xmax = hi), height = 0, colour = "#c3c2b7", linewidth = 2.2) +
  geom_point(aes(shape = sig), colour = col_main, fill = "#fcfcfb", size = 2.3, stroke = 0.9) +
  scale_shape_manual(values = c("spin q < 0.05" = 16, "n.s." = 21), name = NULL) +
  facet_wrap(~syndrome, ncol = 4) +
  labs(x = "r(atrophy, model-predicted atrophy)", y = NULL, subtitle = "Grey bar: central 95% of the spin null (parameters refitted). Schaefer-400.") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

Does any model beat the distance-only baseline? Paired difference r_model − r_distance; two-sided spin p of the difference (both refitted in each spin); FDR across 7 models × 7 syndromes.

  mutate(syndrome = syn_lab(syndrome), model = factor(model, E_models)) %>% arrange(syndrome, desc(diff))
vsD %>% select(syndrome, model, r, r_distance = r_ref, diff, p_spin, q_spin, p_variogram, q_variogram) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)))

11 Extensions (less-applied methods)

11.1 Distance-censored prediction

Local spatial smoothness alone can produce a high r(a, P), because neighbouring parcels have similar atrophy whether or not they are connected. Here each model may only use parcels further than R mm from the target (R = 0–60 mm), so the prediction has to come from distant regions. This removes most of the advantage of any purely local kernel, including the distance baseline, and asks which models still predict atrophy from long-range relationships. The spin null is recomputed at every radius.

cens_models <- c("SC_direct", "communicability", "search_prob", "navigation", "heat", "distance", "FC")
cz <- mt4 %>% filter(model %in% cens_models, syndrome %in% primary) %>%
  mutate(model = factor(model_labels[model], model_labels[cens_models]), syndrome = factor(syndrome, primary))
cz_band <- c4$spin %>% filter(model == "distance", syndrome %in% primary) %>% group_by(R, syndrome) %>%
  summarise(hi = quantile(r, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") %>% mutate(syndrome = factor(syndrome, primary))
cat_cols <- c("#2a78d6", "#eb6834", "#1baf7a", "#eda100", "#e87ba4", "#52514e", "#6250d6")
ggplot(cz, aes(R, r, colour = model)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "#a8a79f", linewidth = 0.3) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(size = 1.6) +
  geom_line(data = cz_band, aes(R, hi), inherit.aes = FALSE, linetype = 2, colour = "#52514e", linewidth = 0.4) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = setNames(cat_cols, model_labels[cens_models]), name = NULL) +
  facet_wrap(~syndrome, ncol = 4) +
  labs(x = "Exclusion radius R (mm): only parcels further than R are used", y = "r(atrophy, prediction)",
       subtitle = "Dashed: 95th percentile of the spin null for the distance kernel") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom") + guides(colour = guide_legend(nrow = 2))

cz_tab <- mt4 %>% filter(R == 30, model %in% cens_models) %>% select(syndrome, model, r, p_spin, q_spin, p_rew_deg, p_rew_geo) %>%
  mutate(syndrome = syn_lab(syndrome)) %>% arrange(syndrome, desc(r))

At R = 30 mm the SC-direct model drops nodes that have no SC edge longer than 30 mm (4 of 400 at Schaefer-400).

11.2 Unique contribution beyond distance

Partial correlation r(a, P_M | P_distance), with the distance kernel refitted for every map and spin surrogate (null: 1,000 spins).

pm <- c("SC_direct", "communicability", "search_prob", "navigation", "FC")
Mlist <- c(communication_models(d4$SC, d4$Dist)[setdiff(pm, "FC")], list(FC = d4$FC))
As4 <- do.call(cbind, lapply(syn, function(s) spin_maps(d4$A[, s], c4$perms)))
part <- do.call(rbind, lapply(c(0, 30), function(R) do.call(rbind, lapply(pm, function(m) {
  obs <- partial_beyond_distance(Mlist[[m]], d4$A, d4$Dist, R)
  nul <- matrix(partial_beyond_distance(Mlist[[m]], As4, d4$Dist, R), ncol = length(syn))
  data.frame(R = R, model = m, syndrome = syn, partial_r = obs,
             p_spin = sapply(seq_along(syn), function(i) p_upper(obs[i], nul[, i])))
}))))
part$q_spin <- ave(part$p_spin, part$R, FUN = function(p) p.adjust(p, "BH")); rownames(part) <- NULL
part %>% mutate(syndrome = syn_lab(syndrome)) %>% arrange(R, syndrome, desc(partial_r)) %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)))

11.3 Comparing null models

The same tests under five nulls. Spatial nulls (spin, variogram-matched, Moran) preserve the map’s spatial autocorrelation; rewiring nulls keep the map and replace the SC by degree-preserving or degree-and-geometry-preserving surrogates.

nl_models <- c("SC_direct", "communicability", "search_prob", "navigation", "heat", "distance")
nl <- mt4 %>% filter(R %in% c(0, 30), model %in% nl_models) %>%
  select(R, model, syndrome, p_spin, p_variogram, p_moran, p_rew_deg, p_rew_geo) %>%
  pivot_longer(starts_with("p_"), names_to = "null", values_to = "p") %>%
  mutate(null = factor(recode(null, p_spin = "Spin", p_variogram = "Variogram", p_moran = "Moran",
                              p_rew_deg = "Rewired (degree)", p_rew_geo = "Rewired (degree + geometry)"),
                       c("Spin", "Variogram", "Moran", "Rewired (degree)", "Rewired (degree + geometry)")),
         model = factor(model_labels[model], model_labels[nl_models]), Rl = paste0("R = ", R, " mm"))
ggplot(nl %>% filter(!is.na(p)), aes(-log10(p), model, colour = null)) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = -log10(0.05), linetype = 2, colour = "#52514e", linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_point(position = position_dodge(width = 0.6), size = 1.5) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = setNames(cat_cols[1:5], levels(nl$null)), name = NULL) +
  facet_grid(Rl ~ syndrome) +
  labs(x = "-log10 p (one-sided); dashed line p = 0.05. Maximum = 3 (1,000 surrogates)", y = NULL) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", axis.text.x = element_text(size = 7))

nl %>% filter(!is.na(p)) %>% group_by(R, null) %>% summarise(tests = n(), significant_p05 = sum(p < 0.05), median_p = median(p), .groups = "drop")

Why the spatial nulls disagree. A null for neighbour-based statistics must reproduce the map’s short-range autocorrelation. The table compares, for each null, the surrogates’ variogram in the five shortest distance bins (ratio to the empirical variogram; 1 = preserved, > 1 = rougher than the real map) and the correlation between each parcel and its nearest neighbour (200 surrogates per syndrome).

vs4 <- variogram_setup(d4$Dist)
nn4 <- apply(d4$Dist + diag(Inf, nrow(d4$Dist)), 1, which.min)
nd <- do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(syn), function(i) {
  x <- d4$A[, i]; g <- drop(variogram(x, vs4))
  sets <- list(Spin = spin_maps(x, c4$perms[, 1:200]), Variogram = sur_v[[i]][, 1:200], Moran = sur_m[[i]][, 1:200])
  data.frame(syndrome = syn[i], null = names(sets),
             short_range_variogram_ratio = sapply(sets, function(X) mean(rowMeans(variogram(X, vs4))[1:5] / g[1:5])),
             nn_corr_null_median = sapply(sets, function(X) median(colcor(X, X[nn4, , drop = FALSE]))),
             nn_corr_observed = cor(x, x[nn4]))
}))
rownames(nd) <- NULL
nd %>% mutate(syndrome = syn_lab(syndrome)) %>% arrange(syndrome, null) %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 2)))

11.4 Geometric vs connectome eigenmodes

Each atrophy map is reconstructed from the first K eigenmodes of three bases: Laplace–Beltrami eigenmodes of the cortical surface (geometric, Pang et al. 2023; fsaverage5, medial wall removed, averaged within parcels), eigenvectors of the normalised SC Laplacian (connectome harmonics), and of the FC Laplacian. Accuracy = r(a, â_K) by least squares; null: 1,000 spun maps reconstructed with the same basis.

eig_K <- c(2, 5, 10, 20, 30, 50, 75, 100, 150, 200)
bases <- list(Geometric = geometric_basis(400), `SC harmonics` = laplacian_modes(d4$SC)$vectors, `FC harmonics` = laplacian_modes(d4$FC)$vectors)
eg <- do.call(rbind, lapply(names(bases), function(b) {
  o <- recon_curve(bases[[b]], d4$A, eig_K)
  nl_ <- recon_curve(bases[[b]], As4, eig_K)
  do.call(rbind, lapply(seq_along(syn), function(i) {
    cols <- (i - 1) * ncol(c4$perms) + seq_len(ncol(c4$perms))
    data.frame(basis = b, syndrome = syn[i], K = eig_K, r = o[i, ],
               null_hi = apply(nl_[cols, ], 2, quantile, 0.95), p_spin = sapply(seq_along(eig_K), function(k) p_upper(o[i, k], nl_[cols, k])))
  }))
}))
ggplot(eg %>% filter(syndrome %in% primary) %>% mutate(syndrome = factor(syndrome, primary)), aes(K, r, colour = basis)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = null_hi), linetype = 2, linewidth = 0.4) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.8) + geom_point(size = 1.4) +
  scale_x_log10() + scale_colour_manual(values = setNames(cat_cols[c(1, 2, 3)], names(bases)), name = NULL) +
  facet_wrap(~syndrome, ncol = 4) +
  labs(x = "Number of modes K (log scale)", y = "Reconstruction accuracy r", subtitle = "Dashed: 95th percentile of the spin null for the same basis") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")

eg %>% filter(K %in% c(10, 20, 50)) %>% select(basis, syndrome, K, r, p_spin) %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = basis, values_from = c(r, p_spin)) %>% mutate(syndrome = syn_lab(syndrome)) %>% arrange(K, syndrome) %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)))

11.5 Smoothness of atrophy on the SC

Normalised Dirichlet energy aᵀLa / aᵀa of the z-scored map on the SC graph (lower = atrophy varies less across strong connections).

sm_obs <- graph_smoothness(d4$SC, d4$A)
sm_spin <- matrix(graph_smoothness(d4$SC, As4), ncol = length(syn))
sm <- data.frame(syndrome = syn, energy = sm_obs,
                 p_spin = sapply(seq_along(syn), function(i) (1 + sum(sm_spin[, i] <= sm_obs[i])) / (1 + nrow(sm_spin))),
                 p_rew_deg = sapply(seq_along(syn), function(i) (1 + sum(c4$rew_deg$smooth[i, ] <= sm_obs[i])) / (1 + ncol(c4$rew_deg$smooth))),
                 p_rew_geo = sapply(seq_along(syn), function(i) (1 + sum(c4$rew_geo$smooth[i, ] <= sm_obs[i])) / (1 + ncol(c4$rew_geo$smooth))))
sm %>% mutate(across(where(is.numeric), ~ round(.x, 3)))

12 Novelty check

Searched on 2026-11-21: PubMed, Consensus (Semantic Scholar/OpenAlex/PubMed), a web search, and an Undermind deep search (102 papers ranked; workspace “Connectome-constrained atrophy: AD vs FTD (communication models)”). The closest papers were then read in full text.

No study found compares structural-connectome communication models (shortest paths, communicability, search information, navigation, diffusion) head-to-head as predictors of atrophy in AD and the FTD variants, against a fitted distance-only baseline, with spatial and rewiring nulls. The closest work:

Study What it did What it did not do
Shafiei et al. 2023, Brain, doi:10.1093/brain/awac069 bvFTD (NIFD: 70 patients, 123 controls, DBM; plus GENFI); SC and FC neighbour atrophy (r = 0.69 and 0.65 at 1,000 Cammoun regions, spin p = 0.0001); anterior-insula epicentre; spin null; geometry-preserving rewiring only for its SIR simulation; 70-subject DSI/fMRI connectome No communication models; no AD, svPPA, nfvPPA; no distance baseline. Our bvFTD neighbour analysis replicates it with an independent connectome (HCP) and parcellation (Schaefer)
Bougacha et al. 2024, Brain Commun, doi:10.1093/braincomms/fcae459 AD (ADNI): ridge regression of atrophy, tau, amyloid, metabolism on SC, FC and cortical-distance predictors (strength, diffusion mode, shortest-path proximity to epicentres), relative importance No pairwise communication models; distance as covariate, not baseline; no spin or rewiring nulls; no FTD
Thompson et al. 2024, Imaging Neurosci, doi:10.1162/imag_a_00089 AD: network diffusion model on five connectomes incl. inverse geodesic distance; FC (r = 0.75) beat distance (0.67) for atrophy; 100 degree-preserving rewired nulls No communication models; no spatial nulls; no FTD
Agosta et al. 2024, Brain, doi:10.1093/brain/awae391 FTD spectrum (bvFTD, svPPA, nfvPPA, sbvFTD): network diffusion model, longitudinal; compared ICVF vs FA connectomes No communication models; no distance baseline; no AD
Garbarino et al. 2019, eLife, doi:10.7554/eLife.49298 AD, MS, ageing: progression profiles combining centrality, shortest-path and spatial proximity to the epicentre No pairwise communication models; no FTD
Brown et al. 2019, Neuron, doi:10.1016/j.neuron.2019.08.037 bvFTD, svPPA: patient-tailored forecasts from FC shortest-path distance and neighbour atrophy Functional connectome only
Zhou et al. 2012, Neuron, doi:10.1016/j.neuron.2012.03.004 Five syndromes; FC epicentres; shorter functional paths to the epicentre predict vulnerability No structural communication models; no nulls of the current kind

Less-applied methods used in the Extensions and their status in this literature:

  • Distance-censored prediction (models allowed only to use parcels > R mm away): not found in the atrophy literature.
  • Comparison of five nulls (spin, variogram-matched, Moran spectral, degree- and geometry-preserving rewiring) for network-constrained atrophy: the null-model literature compares spatial nulls for map-to-map correlations (Markello & Misic 2021, NeuroImage; Burt et al. 2020, NeuroImage), not for network-constrained atrophy. Shafiei et al. 2023 used a geometry-preserving rewired null, but only for a spreading simulation, not for the neighbour correlations or epicentres.
  • Geometric vs connectome eigenmodes for atrophy: geometric eigenmodes have been used descriptively in GRN-related FTD (“mode-based morphometry”, NeuroImage: Clinical 2026); a head-to-head comparison with connectome harmonics across dementia syndromes was not found.
  • Atlas-induced laterality (mirror test): not found.

Caveat: a search can miss work, especially recent preprints and conference abstracts. The claim is “not found in a systematic search”, not “does not exist”.

13 Limitations

  • Different cohorts and pipelines. AD/MCI come from ADNI, PD from PPMI, and FTD and its variants from NIFD. Scanner, acquisition, age, disease stage and control group all differ between maps, so cohort effects are mixed with disease effects in any between-syndrome comparison. The three FTD-variant maps very likely share one NIFD control group, which inflates their mutual similarity (analysis A); spatial nulls do not correct for that. The variant maps also come from a later deposit with a different value scale.
  • Group-level maps. One map per syndrome: no individual variability, no inference across patients; every test is across parcels.
  • Young-adult connectome. HCP SC and FC come from healthy adults aged about 22–35.
  • Cortex only. The Schaefer parcellation omits the hippocampus, amygdala and subcortex. For AD (hippocampus) and bvFTD and svPPA (amygdala, striatum, thalamus) the likely epicentres sit outside the parcellated cortex; cortical “epicentres” here are at best cortical entry points.
  • DBM signal. DBM measures local volume change of the deformation, not grey matter; parcel means near CSF can include sulcal expansion, and depend on upstream smoothing.
  • Template mismatch and atlas asymmetry. Atlas (FSL MNI152, asymmetric) and maps (ICBM 2009c, symmetric) differ, and Schaefer parcels are not left–right homotopic; “Laterality and the atlas” shows this creates spurious left-sided peaks.
  • Spatial nulls disagree. Spin, variogram and Moran nulls give different p-values for the same statistic (see “Comparing null models”); the spin test can be liberal for smooth maps (Markello & Misic 2021). Conclusions rest on effects that survive the stricter nulls.
  • Geometry-preserving rewiring saturates at about 50% edge turnover, so that null is closer to the empirical SC than the degree-preserving one by construction.
  • One fitted parameter for distance. The distance kernel and heat kernel choose their parameter in-sample; refitting inside every null controls the inference, and the tuned-exponent sensitivity analysis gives the communication models the same freedom.
  • connectomeR not used. The functions are project-level reimplementations validated against bctpy, netneurotools and neuromaps, not the package’s own (validated) versions. They should be cross-checked against spin_test(), rotate_parcellation() and rewire_degree() once the 0.2.0 source is available.
  • No DLB. No DLB map exists in the two records, so Lewy body disease is not covered.
